questions.stem: A regional water utility wants Claude to draft replies to customer billing complaints. Discovery has produced 40 requirements, most phrased as ‘the system should handle customer concerns effectively’. The sponsor says the list is thorough and asks you to start building. A colleague proposes three ways to proceed. Which TWO would you endorse? Choose TWO.

options.text: Rewrite the requirements as testable statements with a metric and a threshold — ‘reduce complaint handling time from 14 to 7 minutes’, ‘escalate any account over 90 days overdue to a human’ — because a requirement you cannot measure cannot become an eval case, a design constraint or a release gate.
Schedule a second round of interviews with the customer-satisfaction team, since forty vague requirements suggest the wrong stakeholders have been consulted.
Start with the twenty highest-value requirements and build them, treating the remaining twenty as backlog, so the team makes progress while the list is refined.
Trace each rewritten requirement to the eval case that will prove it, and mark the requirements that have no such case — so the gaps become visible before launch rather than after the first audit.
Send the requirements list back to the sponsor with a request that each item be reworded in the sponsor's own words, since the problem is that the architects wrote them in jargon.

questions.explanation: Both correct moves convert discovery output from **aspiration into evidence**, and they work as a pair. (A) is the conversion itself: a requirement with a metric and a threshold can be tested, can constrain a design decision, and can gate a release. Watch what the rewrite surfaces — ‘escalate accounts over 90 days overdue’ is not a quality aspiration at all, it is an architecture requirement about where the escalation boundary sits, and it would never have been raised as an architecture question in its original form. (D) is the discipline that stops the conversion being cosmetic: tracing each requirement to the eval case that proves it, and **marking the ones that have none**, is what turns ‘we have forty requirements’ into ‘we have thirty-one requirements and nine open questions’ — which is a far more useful document to take to a sponsor.

whyWrong.B: More interviews may well be needed, and stakeholder coverage is part of good discovery. It is not what the stem's evidence points at: forty requirements were produced, which suggests coverage was not the problem — their **form** is. Another round of the same kind of conversation produces more of the same unless the architect brings the question of what each requirement should be measured by.
whyWrong.C: Triaging is reasonable — not everything ships — but you cannot rank requirements you cannot evaluate, so ‘highest value’ is being guessed at. And the items left as backlog keep their vague form, so the backlog becomes a list of things nobody can say whether they are finished.
whyWrong.E: The problem is not authorship or jargon — it is that these requirements contain no observable criterion at all. Asking a sponsor to reword them in their own words would produce forty equally untestable statements, and it hands the architect's job of specifying measurable criteria to someone who does not have the vocabulary to do it.

questions.mindset: A requirement you cannot measure cannot become an eval case, a design constraint or a release gate — convert it before you build.

questions.stem: An insurance group's discovery has surfaced a genuine conflict. The head of claims operations wants the assistant to auto-settle claims under a threshold, because that is where the money is. The compliance lead says every settlement must be reviewed by a qualified human, because settlements are regulated decisions. The architect is asked to ‘find a middle ground’. What is the BEST professional response?

options.text: Do not split the difference — surface the conflict to the decision-maker who owns the regulatory obligation, state explicitly what each party needs, and propose options that all satisfy compliance: the assistant drafts and recommends, a human approves, and throughput gains come from reducing the time the human spends per claim rather than from removing the human.
Auto-settle the lowest-value claims up to a small threshold and require review above it, since a proportionate split is the kind of compromise that keeps both sponsors engaged.
Run a two-week trial with the auto-settling version on claims under the threshold and measure the disagreement rate against human decisions, so the decision is made on evidence rather than opinion.
Escalate the question to the vendor's legal team, since the regulatory requirement is outside the group's control and the vendor should advise on what is permissible.

questions.explanation: A conflict between a **stated regulatory obligation** and an efficiency target is not a trade-off to be balanced — it is a constraint to be satisfied, and the architect's job is to make that clear rather than to produce an agreeable middle. (A) does the three things a professional does here: it does not pretend the tension can be split, it routes the decision to whoever actually owns the regulatory obligation, and it redirects the value claim to something achievable — if settlement time per claim is mostly spent reading the file, then an assistant that pre-reads it and drafts the settlement can cut human effort substantially while the human still approves. That reframing is often where the real value turns out to be.

whyWrong.B: This is the compromise that feels mature and it is the one an architect should most carefully avoid. The regulatory requirement does not have a small carve-out, so auto-settling any regulated decision is a compliance breach with a threshold attached — and the threshold becomes the number that gets quietly raised next quarter, because it is convenient.
whyWrong.C: Measuring disagreement with human decisions is a genuinely useful technique and it is worth doing for many questions — but here it would put a deliberately non-compliant configuration into production, in a regulated process, on real claims, in order to gather data. Evidence does not license that sequence. It is a serious mis-ordering of risk and learning.
whyWrong.D: The group is the regulated entity and carries the obligation; the vendor advises on its own product, not on the group's regulatory position. Escalating internally to the accountable owner is the correct move, and if external advice is genuinely needed then the group's own compliance or legal function is the party to consult.

questions.mindset: A regulatory obligation is a constraint, not a variable to be balanced — route it to its owner and find the value in what remains possible.

questions.stem: A logistics company wants Claude to draft responses to supplier delivery complaints, and has never run an AI project before. A colleague proposes that discovery focus on four questions. Which TWO are the most valuable to ask? Choose TWO.

options.text: Walk me through the last complaint you handled — what came in, what you checked, what you found, what you sent, and how long it took — because a real worked example reveals the actual steps, the actual judgement calls and the actual time cost, which is what the design and the baseline both depend on.
Which Claude model should we use, so that the technical direction is settled before discovery begins.
How much budget is available for the project, since cost determines how sophisticated a solution is appropriate.
Who are the competitors offering this capability, since understanding the market helps us justify the investment internally.

What does a good reply look like and who decides it — because for a company new to this, the definition of done is the one artefact that most reliably becomes the output contract and the first eval cases.

questions.explanation: Both correct answers are about **obtaining ground truth from the people who do the work today**, which is what discovery has to deliver before any architecture is chosen. (A) gets the process, the judgement calls and the elapsed time — the last of which is the baseline the project will be measured against, and the only way to know whether the task needs an agent or a fixed workflow. (E) gets the **definition of done**: for a first project this is the single most valuable artefact, because it becomes the output contract and, with a handful of approved examples, the first eval cases. Everything else in the option set is a decision that discovery should inform rather than a constraint that should frame it — budget in particular invites the team to shape the solution around what they can afford rather than what the work requires.

whyWrong.B: Model choice is downstream of requirements and of a baseline measurement. Opening with it commits budget before you know what the task requires, and it is a question whose answer changes as the organisation learns what the problem is.
whyWrong.C: Budget is a real constraint and should be discussed — but asking it early inverts the relationship between constraint and requirement, and it produces a number without the scope estimate that would give it meaning.
whyWrong.D: Competitive context matters for the internal business case and is a legitimate executive-level question. It is not a question about the task: it tells you nothing about what a complaint looks like, how long handling takes, or where the judgement lies.

questions.mindset: Get a real worked example before any architecture question — it is the only thing that reliably reveals the actual steps, judgement calls and time cost.

questions.stem: A bank's assistant is contractually committed to ‘99% of answers factually correct, as judged by our internal review team’. The team's own eval measures 96.8%, and the contract has a penalty clause. The business owner asks the architect to find a way to reach 99%. What is the architect's BEST response?

options.text: Point out that the clause is written in a currency nobody can price — 'as judged by our review team' — and propose renegotiating it into something operational before launch: a defined eval set, a defined grading protocol, a defined metric, and a severity threshold with human review on the residual.
Accept the commitment and plan to meet it, since a contractual SLA is a hard requirement and the architect's job is delivery rather than renegotiating the terms the business has set.
Propose that the review team grade a larger sample so that the measured figure moves closer to the true underlying rate, which may bring the number within reach of the commitment.
Propose replacing the contractual percentage with a commitment to continuous improvement, with a stated monthly target, since absolute guarantees on model output are not achievable by anyone.

questions.explanation: The clause as written has **no defined measurement procedure**, and that is a bigger problem than the 2.2-point gap. ‘As judged by our review team’ leaves the eval set, the grading protocol, the sampling and even the scoring scale undefined — so the same system can be argued to be at 99% or at 90% depending on who grades what. An architect's first duty here is to make the commitment **operational** before it is signed, and the elements in (A) are exactly the ones that turn a marketing number into a testable obligation. The 96.8% then becomes a discussion about design and review model, which is tractable. Note also that a well-designed version of this contract keeps the severity distinction: 99% of *material* answers correct with human review on the residual is a commitment someone can actually keep and be held to.

whyWrong.B: This is the accommodating answer and it is professionally dangerous. Accepting an unmeasurable 99% guarantee means the architect owns a commitment that has not been defined, cannot be evidenced, and may be assessed against a different method later — in a penalty clause. Raising the definitional problem *before* signature is the whole value of having an architect in the room.
whyWrong.C: A larger sample reduces measurement noise but does not move the underlying rate toward 99%; at best it tells you whether 96.8% was an underestimate. And the stem's problem is not sampling error — it is that the contract does not define the measurement in the first place, so making the sample larger changes nothing about what the clause means.
whyWrong.D: Replacing an absolute number with a continuous-improvement commitment is defensible and it is what some vendors will do — but it is worse for the bank's protection than (A), which produces a real, enforceable commitment the bank can measure and enforce. Abandoning the metric rather than defining it leaves the bank with nothing to hold the supplier to.

questions.mindset: An SLA with no defined measurement procedure is the real risk — make it operational (eval set, grading protocol, metric, severity gate) before it is signed.

questions.stem: A retailer's assistant must give a complete reply within 3 seconds at p95. Engineering's own load test shows p95 at 4.1 seconds and identifies the agent's three sequential tool calls as the cause. The product owner says the SLA is ‘non-negotiable, customers will churn’ and asks engineering to keep trying. Which response is most professionally defensible?

options.text: Bring the evidence back with options and a recommendation — the tool calls are sequential because step two needs step one's result, so name what can actually be changed (collapse calls, cache the lookups, stream earlier output, degrade gracefully) and what each costs in accuracy — and put the remaining risk in front of the decision-maker in writing, since the person who owns churn owns that trade.
Keep optimising until the p95 target is met, since a contractual SLA is a hard engineering constraint and the measurement methodology can be revisited once it is achieved.
Ask the product owner which of the three tool calls matters most to customers, and drop or replace the others, since the customer does not experience the internal call structure at all.
Implement a fallback: if the agent has not answered within 2.5 seconds, return a partial answer plus an offer to continue in a message, so the SLA is met from the customer's point of view.

questions.explanation: The professional position is that an SLA is a **constraint the architect informs, not one the architect silently absorbs**. (A) is that position made concrete: the measurement is in hand, the cause is identified, the dependency structure is explained, and what follows is a set of real options with their accuracy costs attached — collapse the calls, cache the lookups, stream earlier, or degrade. Then the residual risk goes to the person who owns churn, in writing, because an architect who absorbs an unmeetable SLA without recording the decision has converted a business risk into an invisible technical debt. The wording ‘keep trying’ is what this response is for: unbounded optimisation against an unreachable target is how a team burns a quarter.

whyWrong.B: This accepts an unbounded optimisation mandate and defers the methodology question until after the target is met — which conveniently never happens. The deeper error is treating the latency target as purely a technical constraint when part of it is a business choice about whether customers tolerate a slower, more complete answer; nobody has established which.
whyWrong.C: Asking which call matters most is a good product question and it is not a substitute for the technical conversation — but the reasoning in the option is wrong. The customer does experience the consequences of the call structure: whichever call is dropped is usually the one holding the information the customer asked about, so ‘they don't see the calls’ does not mean they don't feel the removal. It also silently decides an accuracy trade without the evaluation that should support it.
whyWrong.D: A partial-answer fallback is a legitimate degradation strategy and a good architect should raise it — as one of the options in (A), with its cost stated. As the answer it is wrong because it meets the letter of the SLA by changing what ‘complete reply within 3 seconds‘ means, without telling anyone. If the commitment's substance is a complete answer, a partial answer plus an offer is a different product, and that is the business owner's decision to make explicitly.

questions.mindset: An SLA is a constraint the architect informs, not one they absorb: bring the measurement, the cause and costed options, and put the residual risk in writing with the person who owns the business outcome.

questions.stem: Three months after an internal HR-policy assistant launches, feedback arrives as anecdotes in a channel — someone says it is wrong about parental leave, someone says it is great. Each time, an engineer adds a sentence to the system prompt. The sponsor asks for ‘the feedback loop going forward’. Which design is BEST?

options.text: Route every complaint into one queue with a required category, then a weekly triage that produces two outputs: prompt changes that go through the eval set before release, and a growing labelled set of real failures that stays separate from the prompt so it remains a genuine test.
Keep the current channel-based process but require that every prompt change be approved by the HR policy owner, since expert sign-off is the main safeguard against regressions.
Have the assistant ask users to rate each answer and review the weekly average with the sponsor, which gives a single number to track improvement against.
Batch the anecdote-driven prompt changes into a monthly release rather than shipping them individually, which reduces the chance of one change masking a regression from another.

questions.explanation: The current process has two structural defects and (A) fixes both. First, anecdotes are **unstructured and unprioritised** — the team cannot tell whether parental leave complaints are one real bug or forty, so effort is allocated by whoever shouted loudest. Second, and more subtly, cases fixed by adding prompt sentences become **cases the prompt has been tuned on** — so if those same cases go into the eval set, the eval stops being able to detect the next overfitting, which is the contamination pattern from the evaluation domain. (A) separates the two roles explicitly: the eval set gates changes, and the growing labelled set stays held-out and stays real. Categorised intake is what makes the volume visible, and the weekly cadence is what stops each anecdote becoming an unplanned release.

whyWrong.B: Expert sign-off on prompt changes is genuinely valuable and should be part of this. It is not a feedback loop though — it is a review gate, and it fixes neither defect: the anecdotes remain unprioritised and unquantified, and the fixed cases still end up in whatever set the team measures with. Sign-off catches a bad change; it does not tell you whether the category of problem is shrinking.
whyWrong.C: A rating average is a single number over a self-selected sample — raters skew to the extremes and most users never rate — so it moves slowly and ambiguously and cannot localise the problem. It is worth having as one signal among several, but the sponsor's question is about the ‘loop’, and a weekly average is a report, not a loop: nothing routes a specific failure back into the prompt or the test set.
whyWrong.D: Batching releases reduces the number of individual changes, which reduces risk per change — real and worth doing. It does not address why the process needs it: the anecdotes are still anonymous, uncategorised and unprioritised, and nothing distinguishes a prompt fix from an index or documentation gap. Monthly batching applied to a stream of unclassified anecdotes just delays the same problem.

questions.mindset: Route complaints into one categorised queue, and keep the eval set held out from prompt tuning — otherwise the loop stops being able to detect the next regression.

questions.stem: A platform team is handing a production claims-summarisation system to the client's operations team, who will run and evolve it. An auditor asks what the handover package must contain. Which set is MOST complete?

options.text: An architecture document with data flow and trust boundaries; the exact deployed configuration including model, prompt and retrieval parameters at handover; the eval suite with its results and the decision rules for release; the runbook covering the failure modes actually observed; and the open risks with their owners.
The source code in the team's repository, a README describing how to run the service locally, and a walkthrough meeting, since code and a walkthrough are the standard engineering handover artefacts.
A written summary of the project's goals, the architecture chosen, the alternatives considered and the reasons for the choice, since the reasoning is what the receiving team most needs.
The eval suite and a monthly quality report, so the receiving team inherits the measurement practice and can see whether quality is holding.

questions.explanation: A handover to a team that will **evolve** the system needs the things that let them change it without breaking it — and that is a different package from the things that let them run it today. (A) has all of them: the architecture with trust boundaries so they know where the risks are; the **exact deployed configuration**, because ‘we use the mid-tier model with this prompt version’ is worthless if they cannot reproduce it; the eval suite with its decision rules, so their changes are gated rather than hopeful; the runbook covering **observed** failure modes, which is what a runbook is for; and open risks with owners, so nothing important is dropped silently. Notice that this is documentation as an operational control, not an administrative artefact — each item prevents a specific class of post-handover failure.

whyWrong.B: Code plus a README plus a walkthrough is the engineering default and it is genuinely necessary — but it is sufficient for a team that will operate the system, not one that will change it. The walkthrough's content evaporates, the README rarely records why a parameter has its current value, and nothing tells the receiving team which changes are risky or which failure modes have already bitten once.
whyWrong.C: Goals, architecture and rejected alternatives with rationale — this is the **decision record**, and it is one of the most valuable documents you can hand over, because it prevents the receiving team from relitigating settled decisions or unknowingly reversing one. It is not sufficient alone: a rationale does not tell someone what the deployed prompt actually says, how to tell whether their change broke something, or what has gone wrong in production.
whyWrong.D: The eval suite plus a monthly report is the measurement half of the package and it is the part most often omitted, which makes it a strong partial answer. What is missing is everything about **operating** the system: no architecture, no deployed configuration, no runbook for the failure modes that have actually occurred, no open-risk register.

questions.mindset: A handover to a team that will evolve the system must carry the eval suite, the exact deployed configuration, the observed failure modes and the open risks — not just code and rationale.

questions.stem: A team has run the same claims system for a year through four prompt changes, a model migration and a new retrieval index. The architecture document still describes the original design, so a new engineer reads it and cannot tell what is actually deployed. Which action is MOST useful?

options.text: Update the document as part of the change — make the deployed configuration and the decision rationale part of what a release requires, so documentation cannot lag behind the system, and record the current state now as a baseline the next change will keep current.
Rewrite the architecture document from scratch to reflect the system as it is today, and schedule a quarterly review so it stays accurate over time.
Keep the original document as a record of the initial design and add a separate ‘current state’ document, since preserving the history of how the design evolved has independent value.
Ask the four engineers who made the changes to write up what they did in a retrospective document, since the people who made the changes know why they were made.

questions.explanation: The failure is not that the document is stale — it is that **nothing in the change process required it to be updated**, so it was always going to drift. (A) fixes the process, not the artefact: if the deployed configuration and the rationale are part of what a release requires, the document stays current by construction, and the rewrite becomes a routine consequence of the change rather than a separate project nobody prioritises. Writing the current state now is what stops the next engineer being misled in the meantime. This is the difference between a document and documentation as an engineering control.

whyWrong.C: Rewriting from scratch and scheduling quarterly reviews is the standard and reasonable remedy, and a careful architect would do it. It is not the MOST useful because it addresses the symptom on a schedule rather than the cause: quarterly review means the document is wrong for up to three months after every change, which is when new engineers are reading it, and the review will be the first thing dropped when the quarter is busy. Making the update part of the release removes the drift instead of scheduling a sweep for it.
whyWrong.D: Keeping the original and adding a current-state document preserves history, which has real value — and history is properly the job of a decision log, not of the architecture document. Two documents covering the same system guarantees a reader eventually consults the wrong one, which is the failure being fixed here.
whyWrong.E: Retrospectives from the engineers who made the changes capture reasoning that nobody else has, and that is genuinely worth having. It is not a substitute for a current architecture document, and it has a structural weakness: it produces one document per change, in the voice and at the depth of whoever wrote it, with no guarantee that the four accounts agree with each other or that anyone checks.

questions.mindset: Fix the process, not the artefact: if the deployed configuration and rationale are part of what a release requires, the document cannot drift.

questions.stem: An architect writes an implementation guide for five product teams who will each build a summarisation feature. The teams differ in document type, language and volume. What should the guide contain MOST?

options.text: The parts that are genuinely common — the input contract, the output schema with a worked example, the eval cases to start from, the cache-breakpoint guidance for a stable prefix, and the failure modes to expect — plus explicit instructions on what each team must decide for itself and what evidence must exist before they ship.
A complete reference implementation for the most typical of the five cases, so teams can start from working code and adapt it, since a worked example is worth more than prose.
A detailed specification of the prompt, the schema and the model configuration, so that all five features behave identically and can be supported as one component.
A list of anti-patterns the architect has seen teams fall into, with a short explanation of each, so teams can avoid the mistakes that have already been made.

questions.explanation: A guide for teams doing **similar but not identical** work should carry the things that genuinely generalise and be explicit about the things that do not. (A) does both halves, and the second half is the one most guides omit. The common core here is real and valuable — an output schema with a worked example, starter eval cases, cache-breakpoint guidance for a stable prefix (which is where most teams lose money without knowing it), and the failure modes — and none of it is document-type specific. But five teams will differ in volume and language, and those differences change model tier, latency budget and retrieval design; a guide that pretends otherwise either over-specifies and gets ignored or under-specifies and leaves every team to rediscover the same lessons. Requiring each team to state its own measurements before shipping is what keeps the guide honest.

whyWrong.B: A complete reference implementation is a genuinely valuable artefact and it is the option a pragmatic architect offers. Its weakness is that teams adapt it by tweaking, so each of the five features drifts from the reference in ways nobody tracks — and the next shared fix has to be applied five times. A worked example of the *output contract* delivers most of the value without handing over five divergent copies of a system.
whyWrong.C: Making all five teams identical sounds like supportability and it would defeat the purpose — the teams differ in document type, language and volume, so a single configuration is wrong for at least some of them, and forcing consistency means either degraded results for some or quiet divergence anyway. Standardising the contract and the measurement practice is right; standardising the whole configuration is not.
whyWrong.D: Anti-patterns are an excellent part of a guide and they should be in it — they are among the highest-value lines per word in this kind of document. But they are advice about what to avoid, not a specification of what to build, and a team that follows every listed anti-pattern still has to work out the architecture for its own document type. Necessary, not sufficient.

questions.mindset: A guide for teams doing similar work should standardise the contract and the measurement practice, and state explicitly what each team must decide for itself.

questions.stem: A regulated lender must show its supervisor, during an examination, exactly why its Claude-based adverse-action drafting assistant produced a specific letter. What must the architecture make possible?

options.text: Per-decision reconstruction: for any letter, retrieve the exact prompt, the retrieved evidence with its source identifiers, the model's reasoning, the tool calls and their arguments, the output, and the model and prompt versions in force at that time — because an examiner is not asking whether the letter was good, they are asking how the decision was reached.
An audit log recording that each letter was generated by the assistant, approved by a reviewer, and filed, since the supervisory requirement concerns the record of actions taken on a credit decision.

A quarterly model card documenting the assistant's training approach, its measured performance across borrower groups, and its known limitations, since that is the standard artefact supervisors expect from a vendor.
An explanation feature in the product itself, so that each borrower who requests reasons receives a clear account of the factors that produced the decision.

questions.explanation: The stem specifies the audience and the question, and they determine the requirement: an **examiner asking how a decision was reached**. That is a reconstruction requirement, and it has to be designed in — the prompt, the retrieved evidence with identifiers, the reasoning, the tool calls, the output, and the version triple, retained per decision. The version triple is the part that is easy to omit and impossible to reconstruct: without knowing which model and prompt version ran, a record cannot be interpreted against the system that produced it, and a later model migration silently changes what every archived decision means. Note the trap in the three distractors — all of them are real artefacts that a regulated lender should have, and none of them answers the question the examiner asked.

whyWrong.B: An action log of generate-approve-file is a genuine regulatory requirement and the lender needs it. It is not what the stem asks for: it records that the assistant was involved and that a human approved, without recording **what information the decision rested on**. An examiner examining an individual disputed decision needs the evidence and the reasoning, and no amount of action logging substitutes for it.
whyWrong.C: A model card is a legitimate governance artefact — fairness across borrower groups, limitations, evaluation results — and it is part of a lender's evidence. It is a description of the **system**, not of a **decision**, so it can establish that the system was evaluated fairly without being able to show why this borrower got this letter.
whyWrong.D: Borrower-facing explanations are an important obligation and often a legal one, and they are a different audience with a different standard — they must be clear and accurate for a borrower, not exhaustive for an examiner. This is a real and valuable feature; it is simply not the capability the examination is asking about, and building it does not discharge the reconstruction requirement.

questions.mindset: An examiner asking how a decision was reached requires per-decision reconstruction — including the model and prompt version, which is the one field that cannot be recovered later.

questions.stem: A team keeps its Claude Code conventions — test command, error-handling pattern, directory layout, forbidden paths — on an internal wiki page. Developers find it and copy the relevant parts into each repository's CLAUDE.md by hand. A colleague proposes two fixes. Which TWO would actually resolve the underlying problem? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move the shared conventions into project-level CLAUDE.md so they are inherited by every repository in that project, with anything genuinely developer- or machine-specific kept out of the repository.
Generate each repository's CLAUDE.md from the wiki page automatically as part of the build, so no developer has to copy anything by hand.
Announce the wiki page in the engineering all-hands and link it from the developer portal, so more developers are aware of it.
Write a short lint that fails a pull request when the repository's CLAUDE.md differs from the current wiki page, so divergence is caught at review time.
Delete the wiki page and rely on each repository's CLAUDE.md as the single source of truth for its own conventions, which is the correct arrangement for a monorepo with heterogeneous services.

questions.explanation: The problem is **N copies of one convention with no update path**, and both correct answers remove the duplication rather than the typing. (A) is the structural fix: CLAUDE.md is loaded hierarchically, so shared conventions belong at project level, a change lands once, and every repository inherits it — which is precisely what hand-copying prevents. (D) works with it because it converts drift from an invisible condition into a **visible failure at review time**, and a stale instruction produces subtly worse work rather than an error, so it needs a mechanism to be noticed. (B) is the tempting one because it removes the effort, and it preserves the defect — generated copies are still copies, so the moment the generator is skipped or a developer edits their local file, the divergence returns.

whyWrong.B: Automating the copy removes the typing and keeps the duplication. Generated files are still per-repository copies, so the divergence returns the first time the generator is not run or someone edits their file locally — and it adds a build step and a template to maintain for a problem that project-level inheritance solves by existing.
whyWrong.C: The stem says developers **do** find the page and copy it, so awareness is not the gap. Announcing it again does not change what happens to the copies after they are made.
whyWrong.E: This confuses per-repository additions with duplicated shared content. A repository can perfectly well add its own service-specific conventions on top of project-level ones; deleting the shared page in favour of N copies is the arrangement that created the problem in the first place.

questions.mindset: Duplicated conventions drift silently; shared ones belong at project level in CLAUDE.md, with anything genuinely local kept out of the repository.

questions.stem: An architect writes an implementation guide for a team that will build an agent which sends supplier emails on the company's behalf. The guide states: ‘outbound email must be approved by a human before sending; never send to addresses not already in the supplier record; log every send with the approver and the content.’ Six months later the team ships something that violates all three. Which is the BEST explanation of why the guidance failed?

options.text: The guide described rules rather than mechanisms — so compliance depended on every prompt, every tool call and every operator remembering them, with nothing that made a violation impossible. The rules should be enforced where the action happens: a hook or the send tool itself requires an approval record and validates the recipient, with logging as a side effect of the send rather than a separate instruction.
The guide was too long for the team to read fully, so the requirements in the last section were the ones most often overlooked.
The guide used prose where the team expected a checklist, so the requirements were not verifiable at the point of implementation.
The guide did not specify which model to use, so the team made inconsistent choices that affected how carefully the rules were followed.

questions.explanation: The three rules in the guide are all correct, all important and all **unenforceable as written**, because nothing made compliance a property of the system. That is the architectural lesson the exam keeps returning to: a control that depends on a model or a developer remembering it is a preference, not a control — and the same principle appears in the capability-bloat, tenant-isolation and permission questions elsewhere in this bank. (A) states the fix precisely. Move the requirement to the layer where the action occurs: a hook in the tool lifecycle, or logic inside the send tool itself, can require an approval record to exist, validate the recipient against the supplier record, and write the audit entry as a consequence of sending. Then a violation is not a mistake someone avoids — it is a request that cannot be fulfilled.

whyWrong.B: Length is a real documentation concern and if the team did not read the guidance that matters. But nothing in the stem suggests selective reading; the more telling clue is that **all three** requirements failed across six months, including one in the first paragraph. A consistent three-for-three failure points at enforcement, not at placement.
whyWrong.C: Format and checkability are genuine design considerations — a checklist is more verifiable than prose — and a careful architect would use them. They do not explain this failure either. A checklist still relies on a person applying it at the right moment; the requirement here concerns an action a model takes autonomously, which is precisely the case prose and checklists cannot cover.
whyWrong.D: Model choice does affect consistency of behaviour, and it is worth specifying. It is unrelated to this failure — there is no plausible mechanism by which the absence of a model recommendation causes a send to go out without approval, and the third requirement (logging) would fail under any model. This is a plausible-sounding issue that does not address the evidence.

questions.mindset: A rule that depends on a model or a developer remembering it is a preference — enforce it where the action happens, in a hook or in the tool itself.

questions.stem: A document-processing system has run in production for a year on one pinned Claude model. Anthropic notifies the team that the model will be deprecated in six months. What is the architect's FIRST concern?

options.text: Whether the migration is behaviour-preserving on their own eval set — because model deprecation is a lifecycle event with a deadline, and the only question that matters is whether the new model passes the same suite at acceptable cost and latency before the date arrives.
Whether the team has a contract with Anthropic about notice periods, since a six-month window may be insufficient for a regulated customer and the architect should establish their position early.
Whether other providers offer a comparable model, so that the team is not dependent on a single vendor for a business-critical process.

Whether the prompt and evaluation suite will need to be rewritten, since every prompt is tuned to the behaviour of a specific model and migration is closer to a re-tuning exercise than a configuration change.

questions.explanation: The deprecation notice creates a **time-boxed migration**, and the first thing an architect needs is the thing that determines whether the migration is safe: a passing eval on the new model. Everything else in the lifecycle — the prompt, the cost model, the rollout — depends on that, and the eval suite is exactly the asset that makes the deadline manageable rather than alarming. Running it early is also the only way to discover the surprise cases: model generations differ in instruction-following and formatting behaviour, so the suite frequently finds regressions that look like prompt problems. The classic migration failure is discovering these in production because nobody ran the suite against the candidate first.

whyWrong.B: Vendor notice periods are a genuine commercial concern for a regulated customer and worth raising with legal — and it is a question for the legal function, not the architect's first technical action. It is also not the binding constraint: a six-month window with a passing eval is comfortable, and a strong eval against a short window is a genuine emergency, so the migration's difficulty, not the contract, is what determines urgency.
whyWrong.C: Vendor concentration is a legitimate strategic question and there are good reasons to explore alternatives. As the first concern in a six-month deprecation window it is a distraction: an abstraction layer across providers is a large project that will not be finished in time and is not needed if the migration passes its eval, which is the likely outcome.
whyWrong.E: This is the pessimistic reading and it is wrong in an important way. Prompts do transfer imperfectly across model generations, which means small adjustments are often needed — but that is a normal part of any model change, not a rewrite of everything. The reason to run the suite first is precisely so you learn how much of this is true for *your* prompts instead of assuming the worst.

questions.mindset: A deprecation notice is a time-boxed migration, and the only question that determines its safety is whether the new model passes the same eval suite.

questions.stem: A bank's assistant has been live for eight months. Last month a customer successfully argued that the assistant told them something incorrect about a fee, and the bank's regulator has asked for an explanation. The team cannot say which system prompt produced the answer, what was retrieved, or whether the answer came from the model or from a cached template. Which lifecycle discipline was missing?

options.text: Per-request provenance retained by default — the model and prompt version, the retrieved sources, the tool calls, and the final response for every request — because the ability to reconstruct a past answer is a property the system must have from launch; adding it later cannot recover the history that has already been lost.
Formal change control, since without an approval step the team cannot establish which version of the prompt was deployed on the day of the incident.
A customer-facing correction process, since the incident would have been resolved faster if there were an established route for retracting and reissuing an incorrect answer.
A formal model-monitoring programme, since a monitor sampling answers weekly would have flagged this class of error before the customer found it.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing detail is ‘**cannot say**— which means the capability was never built, not that it was not used well. Per-request provenance is a **day-one architectural property**: it is recorded when the request happens, and once that moment passes the information is gone permanently. No later retrofits it, which is exactly why the answer here is a lifecycle discipline rather than a process improvement — change control, monitoring and correction processes all presuppose a record of what happened, and none of them can reconstruct it. This is also the same finding as the reconstruction questions in the integration and evaluation domains, seen here from the stakeholder side: an architecture that cannot explain a past answer cannot answer a regulator.

whyWrong.B: Change control with approvals is good practice and would tell you which prompt version was deployed on a given day — useful, and insufficient. It gives you a version, not the answer: not what was retrieved, not which tools ran, not what the model actually returned, and not whether a template path served the request. The regulator's question is about the decision, not the deployment.
whyWrong.C: A correction and retraction process is a real obligation — and it is about what happens **after** an incorrect answer is found. The stem's problem is that nobody can establish what happened at all, so there is nothing to correct or retract with confidence, and no evidence to show the regulator.
whyWrong.D: Weekly sampling is genuinely valuable and it would probably have caught this — but it is a sample. The specific failure is that a single customer's answer cannot be reconstructed at all, and monitoring does not produce per-request records. A monitor plus provenance is the right combination; provenance is the one that was missing.

questions.mindset: Per-request provenance is a day-one property — the ability to explain a past answer cannot be added later, because the history is already gone.

questions.stem: A pilot scored 85% against a 92% target agreed in discovery. The sponsor is disappointed and the CFO asks whether to abandon or fund another quarter. The architect has analysed the failures. What does the architect BEST bring to that conversation?

options.text: The failure breakdown: which categories miss, whether the misses concentrate in a segment, what each class of error costs, and what the 92% target was actually for — because ‘87% or 92%’ is a business decision about which errors matter, and the architect's contribution is the evidence that makes it a decision rather than a disappointment.
A revised timeline with the additional prompt and retrieval work itemised, so the sponsor can see what the remaining seven points will cost.
A recommendation to abandon, since a two-quarter investment that misses its target by seven points is evidence the use case is not viable.
A comparison against a vendor's published benchmark showing comparable performance on similar tasks, which provides useful context for interpreting the result.

questions.explanation: The most useful thing an architect brings to a ‘hit or quit’ conversation is a **decomposition of the error**, because the aggregate is what makes the decision hard. 85% overall could mean seven points of loss spread evenly, or seven points concentrated entirely in one high-value category — and those two situations call for opposite decisions. The breakdown lets the sponsor see which errors they are actually buying, and it puts the 92% target back in front of them as the business judgement it always was: if the misses are cosmetic and the target was set by analogy to another project, a two-quarter push is wasted money; if the misses are the consequential cases, seven points may be unacceptable at any cost. That is a decision the business can make with eyes open.

whyWrong.B: A costed remediation plan is exactly what a pilot report should contain and it is genuinely useful — it is just not the thing that resolves the question being asked. It answers ‘what would it take to get to 92%’ without establishing whether 92% is the right target for this use case or whether the remaining errors are ones anyone should be spending a quarter on.
whyWrong.C: Abandoning on a target miss is a defensible governance stance and sometimes correct. As a recommendation here it is premature and, worse, it discards the analysis the architect already has: seven points is not a verdict until you know which seven points, and abandoning a use case whose errors are all low-value would be a mistake as expensive as continuing one whose errors are serious.
whyWrong.D: A vendor benchmark is the least useful thing on this list, and using it in a go/no-go conversation would be a professional error. Benchmarks describe other tasks on other data; they cannot tell a CFO whether this system's remaining errors are ones their business can absorb, which is the entire question.

questions.mindset: Take an aggregate miss to the business as a decomposed error profile — which errors remain is a business judgement, and the architect's job is to make it a decision rather than a disappointment.

questions.stem: A law firm's internal assistant has been in production for a year. A new firm-wide policy takes effect and changes the answer to a question the assistant is asked daily. Operations asks the architect what to do. Two proposals are on the table. Which TWO would you endorse? Choose TWO.

options.text: Update the source documents and the index, add eval cases that encode the new policy, run the suite and release through the normal gate — because a policy change is the event the feedback loop exists to absorb, and the eval cases are what stop the old answer coming back.
Add the new policy to the system prompt as a temporary override and leave the source documents to be updated at the next scheduled review, since prompt changes take effect immediately.
Escalate to the practice group lead before any change is made, since a legal policy change requires the responsible partner to authorise modifications to a production system.
Pause the assistant for the affected question types until the new policy has been in place for a month, so that partially-updated answers are not given during the transition.
Log every answer given on the affected question type for a month after the change, so that if any of them used the old policy the team has the record and can correct them.

questions.explanation: The endorsement is **change the source of truth and test the change**, plus a way to catch any stragglers — which is what (A) and (E) together do. (A) is the normal iteration loop: update the documents the index and the citations actually point at, add eval cases that encode the new policy so the change is *verified* rather than assumed, and release through the established gate. (E) is the proportionate companion: a temporary, targeted sample of the affected question type, so any answer still resting on the old policy is found by the team rather than by a lawyer who notices — cheap, bounded, and removable. Note that (E) is a detection measure for the transition, not a substitute for (A); without (A) you would just be sampling a system that is still wrong.

whyWrong.B: This is the shortcut to reach for when you need it working now, and it is exactly wrong for a system that will still be running next quarter. Putting the policy in the prompt rather than the documents creates two copies of one rule that then diverge — and the documents are what the index retrieves and the citations point to, so the assistant ends up citing text that contradicts what it says. The next person to update the policy will not know an override exists.
whyWrong.C: Partner authorisation is a reasonable governance expectation for this firm's change control and it should be respected. It is not an alternative to the content change, though — the architect's contribution is what the system should now do about the policy, and the firm's existing approval route applies on top of that.
whyWrong.D: A month-long pause to a capability staff use daily is a large operational cost for a transitional risk the release process already addresses. If staged rollout is warranted it should be per question type and only where the eval shows partial-update risk; a blanket pause is over-reaction.

questions.mindset: A policy change is the exact event the feedback loop exists to absorb — update the source of truth, add eval cases that encode it, release through the gate.

questions.stem: A consulting firm built a client's summarisation service with Claude Code. Two things kept the consultants productive: a repeatable release-review workflow they invoked before every merge, and a project CLAUDE.md capturing the client's conventions and the constraints the client had imposed. The engagement ends and two consultants move to other projects. What is the MOST important thing the firm should do with those two assets?

options.text: Generalise both — strip out the client-specific content from the CLAUDE.md while keeping the structure that made it effective, and generalise the release-review workflow into a firm-wide skill — so the reusable part survives the engagement and the next team inherits a working starting point rather than starting from nothing.
Hand both to the client as part of the handover, since the client owns the service and will continue to evolve it after the engagement.
Keep them in the engagement repository as an archive, since a future team working with this client might need to see what was tried and why.
Document them as case-study material for the firm's sales team, since demonstrable delivery practice is what differentiates the firm in bids.

questions.explanation: The observation the firm should act on is that these are the **two things that generalised** — everything else in the engagement was client-specific by definition. A release-review workflow and a well-structured conventions file are reusable assets that took real iteration to get right, and they are about to walk out of the door with two consultants. (A) captures them before that happens, and does it in the form that transfers: a **skill** is loaded on demand rather than being hard-coded into one repository, so the next team gets the practice without inheriting the client's constraints. The client-specific content has to come out, because a CLAUDE.md that mentions another client's terminology is worse than useless in a new engagement — it will mislead.

whyWrong.B: The client absolutely receives the assets — the service is theirs and they will need both. The question here is what happens **in addition**, because the two consultants are leaving and the reusable practice would leave with them if the firm does nothing. Handing over and generalising are not alternatives.
whyWrong.C: Keeping the engagement repository as an archive is sensible hygiene and worth doing — and it is not what preserves a practice. An archive is discoverable only if someone knows to look, and it contains the client's confidential conventions, so it is also not something a consultant on another project should be reading. Generalising turns an asset into something that is actually applied; archiving leaves it inert.
whyWrong.D: Case-study material is a legitimate commercial use and the firm's marketing team should have visibility of it. It is a downstream benefit of generalising the assets, not the reason to generalise them — and it optimises for the sales narrative rather than for delivery practice, which is the thing the stem identifies as having made consultants productive.

questions.mindset: Generalise the reusable parts before the people who know them leave — a skill travels, an archived repository does not.

questions.stem: A retailer's assistant dashboard has been green for six months: uptime 99.95%, API error rates flat, user complaints low. Last month the retailer added a third-party recommendation widget to the checkout page, and completed-checkout conversion fell 4%. Nobody has connected the two. What does the architect say?

options.text: The assistant's own metrics are the wrong scope for this question — the change is in the surrounding page, not the assistant — so the analysis should start by isolating the assistant's contribution from the page's: replay sessions with and without the assistant against the current page, and confirm the assistant is even present on the checkout path before attributing anything.
Run a prompt change on the assistant to see whether a different tone recovers the conversion, since the assistant's greeting is the last thing the customer reads before the widget appears.
Roll back the widget immediately, since a third-party change is the most likely cause of a 4% conversion drop and speed matters more than evidence.
Add checkout-conversion as a monitored metric on the assistant dashboard, so that any future drop in the metric alerts the assistant team directly.

questions.explanation: The architect's first job is **scoping the attribution**, and the instinct worth resisting is that a green assistant dashboard plus a coinciding metric drop implies a connection. It does not — the change was to the surrounding page, and the assistant's own metrics are flat because the assistant did not change. So the correct move is to establish what the assistant's contribution to the funnel even is on the current page (it may not appear on checkout at all), and to measure that contribution by replaying sessions with and without it. Only after that does a prompt change, a rollout or a rollback become an evidence-based decision. This is the same discipline as the segmented-monitoring questions: a metric moved, and the first question is which population and which layer it moved in.

whyWrong.B: Prompt tuning is the reflex response and it optimises the wrong component — the third-party widget is a page-level change, and there is no established causal path from the assistant's wording to a checkout conversion drop four points wide. Tuning a prompt on a hunch risks degrading a working system while the actual cause stays in place.
whyWrong.C: Rolling back first is defensible when the cost of waiting exceeds the cost of the change, and a 4% conversion drop is a real number. But it is still the wrong order: the widget may be innocent too, the assistant may not be on the checkout path at all, and an immediate rollback can cost money and remove a feature that was performing well. Establish the causal chain before acting on a coincidence.
whyWrong.D: Adding checkout conversion to the assistant's dashboard is a real design mistake in itself: it assigns responsibility for a funnel metric the assistant does not control, and it guarantees future incidents where the assistant team is paged about a page change. If the metric matters, it belongs to whoever owns the page — with the assistant's contribution measured inside it.

questions.mindset: When a metric moves and your own dashboard is green, scope the attribution before tuning anything — the change may not be in your component at all.
